## What Lecture 2.4 Left Open

Lecture 2.4 finished with a defensible sentence about one number: a return of
1.5227 euro a year, a standard error of 0.1897, and an interval that covers the
true 1.30.

Every word of that rests on the five assumptions of Lecture 2.3, and on the
fourth in particular: at every level of schooling, the error averages to zero.

Today is the first lecture in which that assumption is false on purpose. Ability
raises pay, it is not in the data, and people who stayed longer in school have
more of it.

::: {.defn title="Question"}
If the thing you left out raises pay and also raises schooling, is your estimate
of the return too large or too small? Answer before the arithmetic.
:::

## Lecture Plan

::: {.contributions}
1.  **Partialling Out.** What a second variable does to a coefficient, written as a formula you can run.
2.  **Reading a Partial Coefficient.** What holding other things fixed covers, and three variables that break it three ways.
3.  **Omitted Variable Bias.** The gap between the regression you ran and the one you wanted, as a product of two slopes.
:::

# Partialling Out

## The Two-Regressor Model for Earnings and Schooling

We want the return to a year of schooling among people of equal ability, so the
population model carries two slopes rather than one:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 (x_i - 13) + \beta_2 a_i + u_i
\end{equation}
```

- $y_i$: hourly earnings of person $i$, in euro
- $x_i$: years of schooling of person $i$
- $a_i$: ability of person $i$, on the generator's own scale
- $\beta_1$: the return to a year of schooling, holding $a_i$ fixed
- $\beta_2$: the return to a unit of ability, holding $x_i$ fixed
- $u_i$: everything else that raises or lowers earnings

Assumption four now conditions on both regressors at once, $E[u \mid x, a] = 0$,
and the five assumptions are renumbered MLR.1 to MLR.5 [@wooldridge2020].

::: {.defn title="Subscripts on the Slopes"}
Until today there was one slope and $\beta$ needed no subscript. There are now
two. $\beta_1$ is not the $\beta_1$ of Lecture 2.3 even though both are called
the return to schooling: same name, different quantity, different assumptions.
:::

## Ability Is in the Data Only Because We Wrote the Population

No survey of Irish earnings carries a usable measure of ability, and the whole of
section 3 is about what to do when it is missing. It is available today for one
reason only: the generator produced it, so we can read it off.

That makes this section a controlled demonstration. We can run both regressions,
put them side by side, and check by arithmetic what adding the second one did.
Section 3 removes the column again and asks what survives.

A control is any regressor included so that the coefficient you care about can be
read as a comparison at fixed values of it. Nothing about the arithmetic marks a
variable as a control; that is a decision you make and defend.

::: {.caveat title="A Simulation Is Not an Argument About Ireland"}
Every number today is checkable because the population was written rather than
observed. That is what lets us verify a formula. It is not evidence about the
Irish return to schooling, and no frame today claims it is.
:::

## The Part of Schooling That Ability Cannot Account For

A closed form for $\hat{\beta}_1$ in two regressors is not writable in scalars.
What is writable is the variable the regression has left to use, so regress
schooling on ability first:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
x_i = \hat{\pi}_0 + \hat{\pi}_1 a_i + r_i
\qquad\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^{n} r_i = 0
\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i r_i = 0
\end{equation}
```

- $r_i$: the part of person $i$'s schooling that ability leaves over
- $\hat{\pi}_1$: the slope from regressing schooling on ability

The two sums are the first-order conditions of that auxiliary fit, exactly the
pair Lecture 2.1 wrote for earnings on schooling. They say that $r_i$ carries no
ability in it at all [@wooldridge2020].

::: {.defn title="Regression Anatomy"}
$\hat{\beta}_j$ is the slope from a simple regression of earnings on the part of
$x_j$ that the other regressors leave over. The name and the phrase "other things
equal" are both from @angrist2015, and it is the sentence to be able to say back.
:::

## The Two-Step Residual Recipe, Run on Our Own 120 People

Regression anatomy is not a description of what the machine is like. It is an
identity, and it is computable in two lines:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
\hat{\beta}_1
  = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} r_i\, y_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} r_i^{2}}
\end{equation}
```

- $\sum r_i y_i$: the covariance of earnings with the leftover schooling
- $\sum r_i^2$: the variation in schooling that ability leaves over

These are the first numbers of the lecture, and each demonstration today is a
separate run of the generator with one switch on, each with its own population of
200,000 and its own sample of 120. Numbers from two different runs are never the
same regression under different controls.

::: {.worked title="Three Regressions, and the Last Two Agree Exactly"}
Earnings on schooling alone gives 1.5201. Earnings on schooling and ability
together gives 1.1022. Residualise schooling on ability, then regress earnings on
that residual alone, and the slope is 1.1022. The recipe returns the
multiple-regression coefficient to four decimal places.
:::

## Why the Two Steps Return the Same Coefficient

The agreement to four decimals is not a coincidence of this sample. Start from
the long fit, which defines its own residuals, and sum:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i=1}^{n} r_i\, y_i
  &= \sum_{i=1}^{n} r_i \bigl(\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 (x_i - 13)
     + \hat{\beta}_2 a_i + \hat{u}_i\bigr) \\[2pt]
  &= \hat{\beta}_0 \sum_{i} r_i
   \;+\; \hat{\beta}_1 \sum_{i} r_i (x_i - 13)
   \;+\; \hat{\beta}_2 \sum_{i} a_i r_i
   \;+\; \sum_{i} r_i \hat{u}_i \\[2pt]
  &= \hat{\beta}_1 \sum_{i=1}^{n} r_i^{2}
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
```

The first and third sums are the auxiliary conditions from the previous frame.
The fourth is zero because $r_i$ is built from schooling and ability, and the long
fit's residuals are uncorrelated with both in the sample. The second is
$\sum r_i^2$, because $\sum r_i x_i = \sum r_i(\hat{\pi}_0 + \hat{\pi}_1 a_i + r_i)$.

::: {.takeaway title="One Step Carries the Whole Proof"}
The step is the fourth sum. Orthogonality of the long residuals to every
regressor is what removes it, and that is a first-order condition rather than an
assumption about the world [@wooldridge2020].
:::

Some of the variation in schooling has already been used by ability, so what is

:::

## What a Control Costs in Precision

The denominator of the anatomy formula is also the denominator of the variance,
which is why adding a variable and losing precision are the same event:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\beta}_1)
  = \frac{\sigma^{2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} r_i^{2}}
  = \frac{\sigma^{2}}{S_{xx}\,\bigl(1 - R_1^{2}\bigr)}
\end{equation}
```

- $R_1^2$: the R-squared from regressing schooling on the other regressors
- $S_{xx}$: the sum of squared deviations of schooling, as in Lecture 2.3

Lecture 2.3's formula is the case $R_1^2 = 0$. Every control with any predictive
power for schooling raises $R_1^2$, shrinks the denominator and widens the
sampling distribution [@wooldridge2020].

::: {.caveat title="A Control Is Paid For in Standard Errors"}
Unbiasedness and precision are traded here, and the trade is not free in either
direction. Lecture 3.3 gives the extreme case its name; today it is enough that
the price is visible in the denominator rather than asserted beside it.
:::

## A Control That Almost Perfectly Predicts Schooling

Suppose ability predicts schooling almost exactly in our 120 people, so every
$r_i$ sits very close to zero. Nothing about earnings has changed.

::: {.defn title="Question"}
What happens to the standard error on the coefficient for schooling, and which
part of the formula did you reason about to get there?
:::

# Reading a Partial Coefficient

## What Holding Other Things Fixed Actually Covers

Nobody sampled 120 people of identical ability. The data arrived as a random
sample, with ability taking whatever values it took:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
\Delta \hat{y} = \hat{\beta}_1\, \Delta x
\qquad\text{when}\qquad
\Delta a = 0
\end{equation}
```

- $\Delta \hat{y}$: the difference in fitted earnings between two people
- $\Delta x$: the difference in their schooling

Wooldridge's own words are that multiple regression lets us mimic a comparison at
fixed ability without restricting the values of any regressor, and that the data
were not collected in that fashion [@wooldridge2020].

::: {.caveat title="Holding Fixed Reaches Exactly as Far as Your Columns"}
The comparison is between two people who differ in schooling and agree on
ability. It says nothing about anything you did not measure, and it is arithmetic
rather than evidence about what would happen if schooling rose.
:::

## Why Only One Coefficient in Your Table Is Interpretable

Every slope in a two-regressor table is a partial effect, and that is precisely
why the table is not a list of comparable effects:

- $\hat{\beta}_1$ compares people who differ in **schooling** and agree on ability.
- $\hat{\beta}_2$ compares people who differ in **ability** and agree on schooling.

The set of things held fixed is different for each row, so the two numbers answer
two different questions about two different comparisons. Reading down the column
as though each row were an effect of its own variable is a category error.

Only one of them was designed. You put ability in to make assumption four
credible for schooling. Nothing in the model was chosen to make it credible for
ability, and schooling is a mediator for ability: one of the routes by which
ability raises pay is that able people stay in school longer, and $\hat{\beta}_2$
has that route removed.

::: {.takeaway title="The Coefficient You Built the Model For Is the One You May Read"}
Report one coefficient causally and the rest as what they are, the adjustments
that made it credible. A control's own coefficient almost never carries a
defensible interpretation, and it is printed anyway.
:::


<!-- FIGURE 3-1_diagram: drawn, not simulated. Schooling left, earnings right,
     arrow between them. Ability above with arrows down into both. Occupation on
     the arrow from schooling to earnings. Promotion below with arrows into it
     from schooling and from earnings. Colour the three controls differently and
     label them confounder, mediator, collider. No model.R switch needed. -->

::: {.tablenotes title="One Command, Three Different Consequences"}
The same `lm()` call adds all three, and the regression cannot see which is
which. Where a variable sits in the diagram is a claim about the world, and it
has to be argued rather than tested.
:::

## Confounders: Controlling Removes a Bias

Able people stay in school for longer, and they also earn more for reasons that
have nothing to do with school. So schooling and earnings rise together partly
for a reason that is not the return to schooling.

A regression of earnings on schooling alone credits that reason to schooling.
Putting the confounder in removes it: in the anatomy run, 1.5201 with ability
left out and 1.1022 with ability included.

This is the case the phrase "adding controls" was invented for, and it is the
only one of the three in which the coefficient ends up closer to the truth.
Section 3 prices exactly this case, on a different run, once the column is taken
away again.

::: {.takeaway title="A Confounder Causes Both, and Is Caused by Neither"}
That is the test, and it is a test about causal order rather than about
correlation. A variable correlated with schooling and with earnings can equally
well be a mediator or a collider, and those two make the answer worse.
:::

## Mediators: Controlling Removes Part of the Effect You Wanted

Schooling gets a person into a different occupation, and that occupation pays
differently. This is not a nuisance to be removed. It is one of the routes by
which schooling raises pay, and it is part of the number we said we wanted.

This is its own run of the generator, with the occupation switch on and its own
sample. With occupation left out the coefficient is 2.5041. Control for
occupation and it falls to 0.8936, so roughly two thirds of it is gone.

The missing two thirds did not disappear. It is the part of the return that
travels through occupation, and the regression has handed it to the occupation
coefficient instead.

::: {.caveat title="The Smaller Number Is Not the Better Number"}
0.8936 is the return to schooling among people in the same occupation, which is a
real quantity and is not the return to schooling. It deserves the name direct
effect only if nothing unmeasured causes both occupation and pay; if something
does, conditioning on occupation opens the problem on the next frame.
:::

## Colliders: Controlling Creates a Bias That Was Not There

Promotion is caused by schooling and it is caused by earnings. Nothing runs the
other way. This is a third run of the generator, with the promotion switch on and
its own population and sample.

With promotion left out, the coefficient on schooling is 1.1020, positive and
close to the module's true return. Control for promotion and it is $-0.9125$.

The sign reverses. Nothing was omitted from the second regression and nothing was
mismeasured in either. The only difference between the two is the control, and
the control is what produced the negative number.

::: {.caveat title="This Is Why I Controlled for Everything I Had Is Not a Defence"}
Adding a variable made the answer worse, on a population we wrote ourselves. A
defence has to name each control and say which of the three it is, and that claim
cannot be read off the dataset.
:::

## Why the Collider Bias Is Not Sampling Noise

Promotion in this generator is a continuous index built from schooling and from
earnings together. A person reaches a given value of it either by having stayed
in school or by earning well.

So among people who share a value of the index, a person with less schooling must
have arrived there the other way: by earning more. Holding the index fixed forces
schooling and earnings to trade off against each other, and the regression reads
that trade-off as a negative return.

Both regressions were run on the same rows, so the distance between 1.1020 and
$-0.9125$ is not a difference between two samples at all. It is what conditioning
on a common consequence did.

::: {.takeaway title="Conditioning Can Manufacture a Relation That Nothing Caused"}
No arrow in the diagram runs from schooling to earnings through promotion. The
association appears only inside the regression that holds promotion fixed, and it
would appear in a sample of any size [@wooldridge2020].
:::

## What Controlling Does in Each of the Three Cases

Three variables, one command, three results, and only the first is the one the
phrase "adding controls" promises:

- **Confounder.** Controlling **removes a bias**: the part of the association that came from the common cause is taken out.
- **Mediator.** Controlling **removes part of the effect you wanted**: the route through the mediator is taken out with it.
- **Collider.** Controlling **creates a bias where there was none**: conditioning on a common consequence induces an association.

::: {.takeaway title="Two of the Three Are Made Worse by the Control"}
The regression output looks identical in all three cases: a coefficient, a
standard error, a star. Which case you are in is settled by causal order, which is
an argument you make before you fit and cannot recover afterwards.
:::

## Whether Promotion Belongs in the Regression

I want the return to schooling. The dataset has an index of whether the person was
promoted in the last three years, and people high on it both earn more and have
more schooling.

::: {.defn title="Question"}
Should it go into the regression, and what would you need to know about the world,
rather than about the data, to settle it?
:::

# Omitted Variable Bias

## The Regression We Ran and the Regression We Wanted

Section 1 had ability because we wrote it. Take the column away, which is the
situation of every real dataset, and the question is how far that puts the
coefficient we can compute from the one we want:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
\text{long:}\quad
y_i = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 (x_i - 13) + \hat{\gamma}\, a_i + \hat{u}_i
\qquad\qquad
\text{short:}\quad
y_i = \tilde{\beta}_0 + \tilde{\beta}_1 (x_i - 13) + \tilde{u}_i
\end{equation}
```

- $\hat{\gamma}$: the coefficient on ability in the long regression
- $\tilde{\beta}_1$: the slope on schooling from the regression that left ability out

Omitting a variable correlated with schooling is what makes assumption four fail,
and this is the case Wooldridge derives rather than asserts [@wooldridge2020].

::: {.defn title="Hat, and Now Tilde"}
A hat marks an estimate, as it has since Lecture 1.3. A tilde marks an estimate
from a regression that left something out. Both are estimates; only one of them is
estimating the quantity we said we wanted.
:::

## Deriving the Bias in Sample Algebra

The two regressions are run on the same 120 rows, so the gap between them is
arithmetic rather than a statistical claim. Substitute the long fit into the short
formula:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\tilde{\beta}_1
  &= \frac{1}{S_{xx}} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - \bar{x})\, y_i
   = \frac{1}{S_{xx}} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - \bar{x})
     \bigl(\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 (x_i - 13) + \hat{\gamma}\, a_i + \hat{u}_i\bigr) \\[2pt]
  &= \hat{\beta}_0 \underbrace{\frac{\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})}{S_{xx}}}_{=\,0}
   \;+\; \hat{\beta}_1 \underbrace{\frac{\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})(x_i - 13)}{S_{xx}}}_{=\,1}
   \;+\; \hat{\gamma} \underbrace{\frac{\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})\, a_i}{S_{xx}}}_{=\,\hat{\delta}}
   \;+\; \underbrace{\frac{\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})\, \hat{u}_i}{S_{xx}}}_{=\,0} \\[2pt]
  &= \hat{\beta}_1 + \hat{\gamma}\,\hat{\delta}
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
```

The first two braces are Lecture 2.3's two facts about deviations of schooling.
The fourth is the long fit's first-order condition for schooling. The third is the
slope from regressing ability on schooling [@wooldridge2020].

::: {.defn title="The Auxiliary Slope Points the Other Way"}
$\hat{\delta}$ regresses ability on schooling. Section 1's $\hat{\pi}_1$ regressed
schooling on ability. Two auxiliary regressions, opposite directions, different
numbers: the residual recipe needs one and the bias formula needs the other.
:::

## The Bias Is a Product of Exactly Two Slopes

Rearranged, the derivation says the short regression reports the long coefficient
plus one product, and names both of its ingredients:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
\underbrace{\tilde{\beta}_1 - \hat{\beta}_1}_{\text{bias}}
  = \hat{\gamma} \times \hat{\delta}
\qquad
\hat{\gamma}: \text{ ability to pay}
\qquad
\hat{\delta}: \text{ schooling to ability}
\end{equation}
```

A product, so a zero in either ingredient gives no bias at all. A variable that
raises pay but is unrelated to schooling costs nothing. Neither does one that
predicts schooling well and has no return of its own. Both are needed.

The sign follows the two signs. Both positive, or both negative, and the short
slope is too large. One of each, and it is too small [@wooldridge2020].

::: {.takeaway title="The Two Ingredients Are Arguable Separately"}
Each is a claim someone can dispute on its own terms: does the missing thing pay,
and do the people who have it stay in school longer. That is a more useful
argument than a dispute about whether the estimate is credible.
:::

## The Ability Population Is Not Block 2's Population

Block 2 ran the generator with every switch off, and its sample of 120 gave
1.5227, a standard error of 0.1897 and an R-squared of 0.3531, against a true
return of 1.30.

The arithmetic on the next frame comes from a run with the ability switch on: its
own population, its own sample of 120. The short regression there gives 1.6700,
with a standard error of 0.1652, a t-statistic of 10.11 and an R-squared of
0.4642.

::: {.caveat title="1.6700 Is Not What Happens When You Drop a Column From Block 2"}
Two different populations and two different samples, so 1.5227 and 1.6700 are not
a before and an after. The same warning applies to section 1's 1.5201 and to the
two bad-control runs: four separate worlds, four separate draws. The only pair on
this deck that is a before and an after is the next frame's.
:::

## The Formula Closing on Our Own 120 People

The short and the long regression here are run on the same 120 rows, so the
formula is checkable to the last digit rather than true on average:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
\underbrace{1.6700}_{\tilde{\beta}_1}
  \;-\; \underbrace{1.2538}_{\hat{\beta}_1}
  \;=\; 0.4162
  \;=\; \underbrace{0.2206}_{\hat{\delta}} \times \underbrace{1.8867}_{\hat{\gamma}}
\end{equation}
```

A year more schooling goes with 0.2206 more ability, and a unit more ability is
worth 1.8867 euro an hour. Their product is 0.4162, which is the whole distance
between the two regressions, to four decimal places.

Nothing was fitted to make that work. The two ingredients come from two separate
regressions that never saw each other, and the identity is what forces them to
agree [@wooldridge2020].

::: {.takeaway title="The Formula Is an Identity, Not an Approximation"}
It holds in every sample, including ours, for any omitted variable and any sample
size. What is unavailable in real work is not the formula: it is $\hat{\gamma}$
and $\hat{\delta}$, because computing either needs the column we do not have.
:::

## The Short and the Long Slope as Ability Is Made to Matter More

```{=latex}
\fig{../_shared/placeholder.pdf}{The short slope rises with the return to ability; the long slope stays where it is.}
```

<!-- FIGURE 3-1_shortlong: sweep B_04_01, ability to pay, across a plausible
     range with B_04_02 = 0.80 fixed. Plot two lines against that sweep: the
     short coefficient, which rises, and the long coefficient, which is flat.
     Mark the module's 1.30 with a reference line and mark this deck's own point,
     short 1.6700 and long 1.2538. Needs the ability switch on. -->

::: {.tablenotes title="Only One of the Two Lines Rises"}
The long regression holds ability fixed, so the return to ability is irrelevant to
it. The short regression has nowhere to put ability except the schooling
coefficient, and the steeper the return to ability, the more of it lands there.
:::

## Any Pair of Slopes With the Same Product

Suppose someone rejects our estimate and claims the true return is one euro. That
claim has a price: the bias would have to be 0.6700, and the objector owes us a
pair of slopes whose product is 0.6700.

Many pairs do it, and that is the point rather than a weakness. The formula does
not settle an objection; it converts it into two claims about the world that can
be argued separately and, sometimes, checked against other evidence.

In practice the second ingredient is the harder one to defend. Almost everyone
will agree that ability is worth something in pay. Arguing that it is worth three
euro an hour per unit, on a scale nobody has measured, is a different matter.

::: {.defn title="A Bias of 0.6700 Requires Both of These at Once"}
A return to ability of 1.8867 needs an auxiliary slope of 0.3551 rather than
0.2206, which is over half again as much sorting into school by ability. Holding
the sorting fixed instead needs a return to ability of 3.0372.
:::

## What Would Have To Be True?

The claim on the table is that 1.2538 is the return to schooling among people of
equal ability, and that nothing else left out of the model does what ability does.

::: {.defn title="Question"}
What would have to be true for this number to mean what we just said it means?
And what is the plausible story where it isn't?
:::

## Application

The app carries two sliders: how much the omitted variable raises schooling, and
how much it raises pay. The short and the long coefficient are printed side by
side as the sliders are set.

::: {.defn title="Question"}
With both sliders at their midpoint, is the short estimate above the long one,
below it, or the same? Then set either slider to zero and answer again.
:::

The lab for this lecture is the residual recipe: `resid()`, then `lm()`, checked
against the two-variable `lm()`, and then the same check for the bias formula.

## Summary: Partialling Out, Bad Controls and Omitted Variable Bias

::: {.contributions}
1.  **Partialling Out.** A coefficient is the simple-regression slope on the part of a variable the other regressors leave over, which on our sample is 1.1022 either way.
2.  **Reading a Partial Coefficient.** Each row holds a different set of things fixed, and a control can remove a bias, remove part of the effect, or reverse the sign.
3.  **Omitted Variable Bias.** Short minus long is $\hat{\gamma}\hat{\delta}$, which on our 120 people is $0.2206 \times 1.8867 = 0.4162$.
:::

## Next Lecture

Lecture 3.2 keeps today's machinery unchanged and replaces the variables that go
into it:

- **Logs and Elasticities:** change the units and the coefficient answers a different question.
- **Dummy Variables:** a category shifts the intercept, relative to a base you chose.
- **Interactions:** let the slope differ across groups, and every coefficient around it is read differently.

Regression anatomy carries over intact. A dummy variable is residualised in
exactly the way ability was today, and the interpretation of an interaction is
read off the same partial-effect rule.

## {.plain}

::: {.appendix}
:::

## Derivation: The First-Order Conditions for Two Regressors

The anatomy proof used three conditions on the long fit's residuals without
obtaining them. All three come from differentiating the sum of squared residuals
and setting each derivative to zero:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
\sum_{i=1}^{n} \hat{u}_i = 0
\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - 13)\,\hat{u}_i = 0
\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i\, \hat{u}_i = 0
\end{equation}
```

::: {.takeaway title="One Condition per Coefficient"}
Three coefficients give three conditions, which is why the divisor for
$\hat{\sigma}^2$ is $n-3$ here and was $n-2$ in Lecture 2.3. Wooldridge writes the
general set for $k$ regressors as $k+1$ equations [@wooldridge2020].
:::

## Derivation: Why the Centring Constant Cancels

Both body derivations used $\sum (x_i - \bar{x}) = 0$ and
$\sum (x_i - \bar{x})(x_i - 13) = S_{xx}$, proved in the appendix to Lecture 2.3:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - \bar{x})(x_i - 13)
  = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - \bar{x})^{2}
  + (\bar{x} - 13)\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - \bar{x})
  = S_{xx}
\end{equation}
```

::: {.takeaway title="Centring at the Leaving Certificate Costs Nothing"}
The second sum is zero, so the 13 contributes nothing and both derivations run
unchanged on raw schooling. Centring sets what the intercept means and leaves
every slope on this deck where it was.
:::
